title: Google Cloud brings AlphaEvolve to GA and ships agentic HPC skills ahead of SC26
subtitle: The DeepMind evolutionary code optimizer lands generally available on Cloud Batch alongside a library of "agentic HPC skills" for OpenFOAM, STAR-CCM+, GROMACS, AlphaFold 3 and OPM — with mandatory human-approval gates.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Ahead of SC26 in Chicago, Google Cloud took AlphaEvolve — the DeepMind evolutionary code optimizer built on Gemini — to general availability on Cloud Batch, and released a set of agentic HPC skills to the Google Skills and DeepMind Science Skills repositories. The skills are composable, with self-describing deterministic tools and end-to-end automated testing. Domain coverage at launch includes configuring OpenFOAM and Siemens STAR-CCM+ fluid-dynamics runs, tuning GROMACS and AlphaFold 3 life-sciences pipelines, and launching Devito and Open Porous Media subsurface simulations. Google is demoing the stack — Antigravity for HPC, the HPC Prompt Playground, and AlphaEvolve for HPC — at booth 3418 at McCormick Place West through November 20.

The design choice that matters here is the guardrail. Google's blog explicitly says agentic HPC isn't about turning unguided models loose on a cluster terminal: skill invocations require human approval, and the deterministic-tool wrapper is there to make agent actions auditable. That's a departure from the generic coding-agent pattern, where the agent decides what to run and when. On an HPC cluster, a bad decision costs a six-figure job, so the review step is load-bearing.

AlphaEvolve itself has been in preview since earlier this year, where DeepMind reported it finding faster matrix multiplication algorithms and improved data-center scheduling heuristics. The Cloud Batch GA brings it into normal engineering workflows: a user points it at a codebase and a cost or runtime objective, and the system evolves candidate implementations. The HPC skill library is meant to let the same agent pattern work across the surrounding scientific stack — not just the inner optimization loop.

A note for learners: the agentic HPC pattern is a useful template even if you never touch a supercomputer. Narrow, deterministic tools with explicit human-approval gates give you most of the value of autonomous agents, with far fewer of the safety problems. If you're building any agent today, the two design questions to ask first are: what are the tools, exactly, and where does the human sign off? Google's SC26 stack is a worked example of what good answers look like.
